overview.text: Melatonin is a hormone made by the pineal gland in the brain. It acts as a time signal linking the light–dark environment with the body’s internal clock: light information reaching the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) helps control its production, which normally increases after dark and falls in daylight. This daily pattern helps set the timing of circadian rhythms—roughly 24-hour cycles that shape sleep patterns and other bodily functions. Melatonin can signal readiness for sleep, but it is not an on/off switch required for sleep. The body’s natural hormone rhythm is distinct from melatonin taken as a supplement, whose usefulness depends on the condition.

key_facts.text: The pineal gland releases more melatonin at night as light entering the eyes diminishes; light exposure can reduce its production.
The SCN, a group of nerve cells in the brain, helps control melatonin production based on light information received from the eyes.
Circadian rhythms are roughly 24-hour cycles and influence sleep patterns, hormone release, appetite and digestion, and body temperature.
Melatonin signals the body to prepare for sleep, but it is not necessary for a person to sleep.
Melatonin supplements are distinct from the hormone naturally produced by the body; most supplements are made synthetically.
